title: Prefill vs Decode Pipeline: Overlap, Micro-batching, Stream Priorities (Draft)
content:
Purpose
This note captures design considerations for splitting and/or overlapping the "prefill" and "decode" stages in the Redwood serving runtime. Focus areas: micro-batching strategies, stream prioritization, KV-cache semantics, and kernel/scheduling interactions. This is a draft for discussion with serving-runtime, release-engineering, and SRE.

Background
- Prefill: compute full attention / KV cache for the prompt context and produce initial KV caches. Typically expensive (long sequences, multi-GPU) but can be batched across requests that share similar sequence lengths.
- Decode: autoregressive generation that consumes KV cache and runs stepwise attention. Latency-sensitive, benefits from small-batch/streaming optimizations and fast kernel paths.

Goals
- Reduce end-to-end tail latency for interactive/streaming requests while maintaining high throughput for high-volume batched workloads.
- Maximize GPU utilization via micro-batching where possible without violating latency SLOs.
- Ensure correctness and memory safety of KV cache when prefill and decode overlap or execute on different devices.

High-level approaches
1) Strict separation (baseline)
   - Prefill runs to completion, writes finalized KV caches to storage (in-memory or device-local), then decode consumes them.
   - Simple semantics, easy kernel selection and scheduling, but underutilizes opportunities to overlap compute and hide latency.
2) Overlapped pipeline (proposed)
   - Start decode for the earliest finished segments of a request while other parts are still prefill-ing (e.g., for streaming prefixes, or multi-chunk context uploads).
   - Requires partial KV cache visibility and safe handoff semantics.
3) Hybrid with staged micro-batch slots
   - Maintain a scheduler that groups requests by decode readiness and sequence length; allows small micro-batches for decode layered on top of larger prefill batches.

Key design components
A) KV cache semantics and handoff
- Represent KV cache as append-only per-layer tensors indexed by token position (device-resident whenever possible).
- Partial readiness: permit decode to start once the prefix KV slices [0..k] are available for all required layers. Decode must only read positions <= k.
- Consistency: if prefill continues to emit earlier KV positions (due to reordering), scheduler must enforce memory barriers or versioned handles.
- Device placement policy: prefer producing KV on the device that will run decode to avoid cross-device copy. If prefill runs on a different device, we implement async copy with pipelined DMA and backpressure.

B) Micro-batching strategies
- Prefill batching: batch by prompt length buckets (e.g., 64/128/512 tokens) and model parallel placement. Larger batches maximize throughput and kernel efficiency.
- Decode micro-batching: maintain a low-latency window (e.g., 8-32 concurrent tokens across requests) and use continuous batching to aggregate tokens across active streams.
- Cross-stage microbatching: allow a small decode batch to be scheduled whenever sufficient partial KV slices are available from multiple requests to amortize kernel launch costs.
- Timeouts and latency SLOs: scheduler should enforce decode dispatch if waiting time exceeds threshold even if batch size is suboptimal.

C) Stream priorities and preemption
- Priority classes: interactive (low-latency), streaming (moderate), batch (best-effort). Incoming requests tagged at admission (policy or API hint).
- Prefill scheduling: batch-oriented, lower priority for interactive requests unless prompt is short. For interactive requests we can favor prefill on-device to speed handoff.
- Decode scheduling: highest priority for interactive/streaming; decoder micro-batches preempt long-running prefill jobs where possible.
- Preemption mechanics: soft preemption via cooperative yield points in large prefill kernels (split long sequence prefill into chunks that yield to decoder work). Hard preemption only for exceptional situations (OOM protection).

D) Kernel selection and performance
- Prefill kernels favor dense, high-throughput matmul kernels and fused attention for long sequences. Optimize for large batch sizes and sequence-parallel memory layout.
- Decode kernels favor low-latency single-step attention and optimized KV gather/scatter operations. Kernel launch overhead matters: use persistent kernels or CUDA graph capture for steady-state streaming.
- When overlapping, choose kernels that minimize cross-device memory traffic. Example: if prefill on device 0 but decode on device 1, prefer smaller prefill blocks and early copies to device 1 for initial KV slices.

E) Scheduler model
- Job descriptors: prefill job (request id, sequence length, preferred device, priority, batch bucket), decode job (request id, current token position, readiness flag, priority).
- Readiness predicate for decode: bool ready = (kv_slices_available(request, up_to_position)) && (gpu_memory_available(predicted_decode_work)).
- Allocation policy: try to collocate prefill and decode on same device for interactive requests if it reduces data movement and meets utilization targets.

Metrics and observability
- E2E latency by priority class (p50/p95/p99), prefill time, decode time, overlap ratio (fraction of decode time overlapped with other prefill work), GPU utilization, cross-device memcpy time, average micro-batch sizes.
- Traces should include KV cache handoff events and version ids to debug partial-read issues.

Implementation risks and mitigations
- Race conditions on KV partial reads: mitigate with versioned handles and atomic readiness flags.
- Memory pressure from holding multiple partial KV caches: enforce per-request limits and spill to host for low-priority jobs.
- Kernel incompatibility for overlapped execution: provide a compatibility matrix and fallback to strict separation if necessary.

Open questions
- How to generalize readiness thresholds across different model sizes and quantization profiles?
- What are the appropriate default micro-batch windows for medium-sized pods (4–8 GPUs)?
- Can we leverage CUDA Graphs to capture both prefill and decode kernels to reduce overhead in overlapped execution?

Next steps
- Prototype a minimal overlapped pipeline for 7B/13B models on single-GPU: implement partial-KV handles, decoder readiness predicate, and micro-batcher for decode.
- Run perf runs comparing strict separation vs overlapped for interactive workloads (websocket streaming) and batch workloads (bulk embeddings + long-context generations).
- Sync with kernel/compilation team about persistent kernel work and CUDA Graph feasibility.

Appendix: quick glossary
- KV cache: per-layer key and value tensors used to avoid recomputing attention for previously-seen tokens.
- Prefill: initial forward pass over prompt context to build KV cache.
- Decode: iterative autoregressive generation using existing KV cache.
- Micro-batching / continuous batching: batching small amounts of work across active streams to improve GPU efficiency while preserving latency.

End of draft.
